newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reserves move seen supporting rouble.
newsitem.headline: Russian reserves move seen supporting rouble.

text.p: Russia adjusted banks' reserve requirements on Friday, in a move which will strengthen the rouble, push down yields and help the central bank build up its foreign exchange reserves, bankers said.
The central bank shaved reserve ratios on short-term rouble accounts but doubled the ratio on hard currency accounts.
"The situation with stabilising inflation and the rouble rate allows us to set new paramters for banking system development," central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin told a news conference.
Inflation was 0.3 percent in July after prices fell 0.2 percent in August. It is likely to be 1.2 percent in October.

Last week, the central bank cut its refinancing and Lombard rates. Yields on the T-bill market have fallen to about 50 percent after topping 200 percent just before this summer's presidential election.
The central bank has succeeded in holding the rouble/dollar rate within the sloping corridor introduced this summer.
The sloping corridor is a form of crawling peg, in which the rouble is guided down over the year at a pre-set rate.

"This is a measure to strengthen the rouble," said Dmitry Vinogradov, Alfa-Bank deputy chairman. "Banks will not have difficulties meeting the new requirements, and it will not worsen their financial situation."
Nevertheless, the central bank gave banks until November 11 to adjust to the new ratios on foreign currency, which officially come into force on November 1.
Dubinin said the central bank was worried by its falling net international reserves.
"We are making the process of holding funds in dollars more expensive," Dubinin said. "We are consciously pushing banks to sell hard currency."
In August, the central bank sold $1 billion on the interbank market following serious borrowing by foreign banks on the Treasury-bill market.
Pavel Teplukhin, chief analyst at Troika Dialog, said the change would help the central bank preserve its policy of a gentle depreciation of the rouble.
"The rise in reserve requirements for hard currency accounts will lead to a transfer of some hard currency deposits into rouble ones," he said.

The effect on the currency market would only be short-term, because most banks hold more funds in the central bank than necessary by reserves requirments, as they have to use the central bank as the biggest clearing centre, he said.
The change could also push down the yields on the government securities market, by increasing the supply of roubles looking for an investment haven.
Lower domestic yields and interest rates could also encourage some companies to pay taxes rather than hold money on deposit, he said.
Poor tax collection is the main economic problem in Russia, where tax revenues have so far this year amounted to little more than 70 percent of targeted levels.

This was the main sticking point in talks between Russia and the International Monetary Fund on payment of the next tranche in Russia's $10 billion IMF loan, which ended on Thursday without agreement.
The central bank made the following changes in reserve ratios from November 1:
* rouble accounts 1-30 days -- 16 pct (18 pct)
* rouble accounts 31-90 days -- 13 pct (14 pct)
* rouble accounts 90 days and over -- 10 pct (same)
* currency accounts all maturities 5.00 pct (2.50 pct)
